So don't stress about moats, for example. Just grow. It's slightly bad not to have a moat, but it's far worse to pass on an opportunity to grow because it doesn't have one. Moats often emerge later anyway.

In some respects AI has made the standard startup advice even more true. For example, one thing we tell startups is not to be conservative, because they have nothing to lose. Since they can move fast, they should. This is even more important now.

One change is that you don't always need a cofounder to help you do the work, because AI can do a lot of it. But helping you do the work was never the main reason to have a cofounder. You need a cofounder to help bear the stress. AI can't do that for you.

One question founders always ask when we speak at YC is: How much of the standard startup advice still applies in the age of AI? At this point, nearly all of it. I can't promise that will be true in 10 years, but at this moment, starting a startup is much the same as always.
If customers won't buy your stuff, try asking what they would buy. This sounds obvious, but surprisingly few founders do it, and it often yields valuable insights.

The movement in this watch is a famous one, the AP cal 2120, which is in turn based on the JLC cal 920.  When it was launched in 1967 it was the thinnest full-rotor automatic movement ever made, at 2.45 mm. It still is.

Since this movement is a self-winding one, there's a rotor on the other side. It's the gold semi-circle occupying the bottom half of the movement. This rotates as you move your arm, keeping the watch wound. You want a rotor to be dense, so this one is 21k gold. https://t.co/qtrQrcPN8v

This skeletonized Audemars Piguet 14232 is a great way to understand how movements work. The big circle at 1:00 is the muscle: the barrel, which contains the mainspring. The other, at 5:30, is the brain: the balance wheel, which oscillates rapidly to keep time. https://t.co/OgA0hl9HJr

Your usage restrictions are my opportunity.

Any business that bans agents represents an opportunity for a startup to create a competitor. If they need to ban agents, it must mean people want to use them, or there would be no point. And that in turn means there's demand for a competitor that allows them.

Amazon banning agents is the first opportunity I've seen since Amazon was founded for a startup to create an Amazon competitor. People will want agents to buy stuff for them. It will be one of the main use cases. And they won't want to use some Amazon-supplied agent to do it.

Nasty problems aren't completely useless though. So-called "real world" problems are often nasty problems. So working on them is often a good way to make money, or to make people's lives better. Just don't choose one by accident.

If I had to say in one word what distinguishes the juicy ones, the word might be unity. Nasty problems tend to be collections of random, often extrinsic constraints. Juicy problems have one main thing you're trying to solve

One very important thing that even the smartest people seem to have to learn from experience is taste in problems. There are juicy problems that tend to lead to interesting discoveries, and nasty problems that tend not to.
